title: Choosing a clay body for your project
subtitle: Matching clay type to the demands of what you are making
excerpt: Different clay bodies are suited to different projects. Air-dry clay, polymer clay, paper clay, stoneware, porcelain, and earthenware each have distinct properties that make them better or worse for specific uses. Choosing the wrong clay body at the start is the most common cause of projects that crack, warp, or don't survive use.
sourceNotes: Clay body selection criteria synthesised from standard ceramics technical reference. Properties and use-case mapping derived from technical properties of each clay body type.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process during kiln firing where clay particles fuse together into a glass-like matrix, making the clay dense, strong, and non-porous.
Pre-fired, ground clay particles added to a clay body to reduce shrinkage and improve resistance to cracking during drying and firing.
The reduction in size a clay body undergoes as it dries and fires. Most clays shrink 10 to 15 percent from wet to fired.

content.text: Clay body choice determines whether a finished piece is waterproof, food-safe, strong enough for its intended use, and compatible with the decoration techniques you want to apply. No single clay body is best for everything. This tutorial maps the common clay bodies to the project types they suit, so you can match the material to the outcome from the start.
No-kiln clay bodies
Air-dry clay is suited to decorative objects, flat tiles, picture frames, and lightweight sculptural pieces. It is not waterproof and is not suitable for functional vessels without sealing.
Shrinkage
is lower than kiln-fired clays: around 5 to 8 percent when dry: which makes warping less common in flat pieces. Fragile in thin sections.

Polymer clay is suited to small decorative objects, jewellery, earrings, pendants, and keyrings. It does not shrink on curing, which makes it suitable for precise small work. Not suitable for large flat slabs (warps on curing) or food-contact use. Requires oven curing at 110 to 130 °C, not a pottery kiln.

Paper clay (air-dry base) is air-dry clay with paper fibres added. The fibres dramatically reduce cracking in large flat slabs and large sculptural forms. Best choice for large decorative projects, relief sculptures, and flat tiles where air-dry clay alone would crack. Still not waterproof without sealing.
Kiln-fired clay bodies
Earthenware fires at cone 06 to cone 2 (around 1000 to 1160 °C). Remains porous at these temperatures: not fully
vitrified
: so earthenware must be glazed inside for food or liquid contact. Best for decorative tiles, sculptural pieces, and traditional slipware. Less suited to outdoor use (frost-vulnerable).

Stoneware fires at cone 6 to cone 10 (around 1220 to 1300 °C). Denser and stronger than earthenware at temperature: approaches vitrification. Suitable for functional mugs, bowls, plates, and storage crocks. More forgiving on the wheel than porcelain.
Grogged
stoneware (with added grog) handles better for hand-building large forms.

Porcelain fires at cone 8 to cone 10 (around 1260 to 1300 °C). Translucent when thin; fully vitrified and completely non-porous when fired. Suited to fine tableware, precise thrown forms, and sculptural work where translucency is wanted. Demanding to throw: requires centring skill and patience. High shrinkage (12 to 15 percent) means measurements must account for size reduction.
Match to purpose
Decorative indoor object, no water contact: air-dry clay or paper clay.
Jewellery and wearable items: polymer clay (small, precise, no shrinkage).
Functional mug or bowl (kiln): stoneware: durability and ease of throwing or hand-building.
Fine thrown tableware (kiln): porcelain: translucency and full vitrification.

Clay body choice affects how the piece performs. It sets whether the piece is waterproof, food-safe, and strong enough. It also affects which decoration techniques work. No single clay body suits every project.
Large sculptural form (no kiln): paper clay: fibres prevent cracking during drying.

rows.problem: Piece cracked during drying even though clay was chosen for the project type
rows.cause: Uneven wall thickness; one section drying faster than another
rows.fix: Even wall thickness is as important as clay body choice. Roll slabs between guide rails; throw walls to consistent gauge throughout.

rows.problem: Finished piece absorbs water even after glaze firing (earthenware)
rows.cause: Glaze did not cover the full interior; or fired below the glaze's maturing temperature
rows.fix: Apply glaze to the full food-contact interior surface. Confirm your kiln is reaching the glaze's specified cone temperature with a witness cone.
